extracted.intended_audience: systematic review authors and meta-analysts (especially Cochrane review authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting effect measures and extracting data for dichotomous and continuous outcomes when conducting meta-analyses, including how to derive or impute missing variance measures and how to handle different measurement scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of odds ratios versus risk ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Odds ratios can be misleading when events are common: they will tend to overestimate the intervention effect, especially when events are common (with, say, risks of events more than 20%). For interventions that reduce the chances of events, the odds ratio will be smaller than the risk ratio, so that, again, misinterpretation overestimates the effect of the intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when using odds ratios for interpretation; prefer risk ratios or risk differences for clearer clinical interpretation when events are common. Explicitly note the potential for overestimation and avoid misinterpreting odds ratios as risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of absolute effect: the risk difference
rubrics_metrics.description: The risk difference is the difference between the observed risks (proportions of individuals with the outcome of interest) in the two groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk difference is straightforward to interpret and useful for trade-offs between benefits and harms, but clinical importance depends on underlying baseline risk (e.g. 2% can be trivial or important depending on baseline). It is constrained by possible probability bounds, which can make application to populations with different baseline risks problematic (e.g. a risk difference of –0.1 applied to a group with 7% baseline risk gives an impossible negative probability). The number needed to treat (NNT) is obtained from the risk difference; NNTs cannot be combined in a meta-analysis, though relative measures may be converted to NNTs for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and definition of the event for dichotomous outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: In dichotomous outcomes an 'event' describes the outcome or state of interest (e.g. recovery, onset of disease). It is possible to switch events and non-events, but this may affect effect measures differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide before analysis which state is the event (often the change in state or the less common state). Switching event/non-event has little consequence for risk differences and odds ratios (sign change or reciprocal), but can substantially affect risk ratios, their precision, significance, and heterogeneity. A rule of thumb: focus on the less common state to reduce extrapolation problems and potentially reduce heterogeneity. Where interventions aim to reduce an adverse event, risk ratios of the adverse event are empirically more consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data required for dichotomous outcomes (2×2 table)
rubrics_metrics.description: To calculate summary statistics and include a dichotomous result in a meta-analysis, the numbers of participants in each intervention group who did and did not experience the outcome (the 2×2 table) are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer collecting numbers of actual observations (number measured) rather than reported totals (which may be ambiguous). When only percentages are reported, derive numerators cautiously (rounded percentages can map to multiple numerators). If only effect estimates (odds ratio, risk ratio) are reported, include them only if accompanied by uncertainty measures (SE, 95% CI or exact P value) and use the generic inverse variance method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect measures for continuous outcomes: mean difference (MD)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean difference (difference in means) measures the absolute difference between the mean value in two groups and estimates how much, on average, the experimental intervention changes the outcome compared with the comparator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MD when outcome measurements in all studies are made on the same scale. Be aware that 'weighted mean difference' is a historical term; MD is the preferred terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect measures for continuous outcomes: standardized mean difference (SMD)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standardized mean difference (SMD) is used when studies assess the same outcome but measure it using different scales; it expresses the intervention effect relative to the between-participant variability (SD) in each study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SMD to combine different instruments, but ensure all scales point in the same direction (flip scales as needed) and report any reversals. The SMD assumes differences in SDs across studies reflect scale differences rather than true population variability—this assumption may be violated (e.g. pragmatic vs explanatory trials), affecting comparability and interpretation. The Cochrane-preferred SMD is Hedges' g (pooled SD denominator). Consider alternatives (Glass' Δ using comparator SD; external SDs when appropriate). Report any adjustments in statistical methods. Remember interpretability is in SD units; use options (Chapter 15) to aid clinical interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory expectation when combining different scales (MECIR C61)
rubrics_metrics.description: If studies are combined with different scales, ensure that higher scores for continuous outcomes all have the same meaning for any particular outcome; explain the direction of interpretation; and report when directions are reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining scales with opposite clinical meaning creates meaningless or misleading results. Explicitly describe any direction reversals and ensure higher scores consistently reflect either better or worse outcomes across included studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variants of SMD and choice of SD denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: Different SMD variants exist depending on the choice of SD for the denominator (pooled SD as in Hedges' g, comparator-group SD as in Glass' Δ, or an external SD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose variant based on assumptions about whether the intervention affects variability and on availability of reliable SD estimates. External SDs (from large cohorts) may be used when within-study SD estimates are unreliable; then analyze as MDs with divisor equal to external SD. Document and justify the choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratio of means (RoM) for continuous outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of means (RoM) measures the relative difference between group means (the average is multiplied by RoM for the experimental group vs comparator).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RoM suits outcomes that can only be positive and when different measurement approaches cannot be converted. It requires comparable lower limits across scales (otherwise RoM ranges differ and comparisons are invalid). RoM is suitable for single post-intervention assessments but not for change-from-baseline measures (which can be negative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other continuous effect measures and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Other measures include standardized difference expressed in terms of minimal important differences (MID), prevented fraction, difference in percentage change from baseline, and direct mapping between scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose these alternatives when they improve clinical interpretability or match historical use; take care with SE calculations (e.g. percentage change needs correct handling of correlation between baseline and post measures). Use conversion factors or mapping methods when available; document methods used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required data for continuous outcome meta-analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: To perform meta-analysis using MDs, SMDs or RoM, review authors should seek: the mean value of the outcome in each intervention group; the standard deviation of the outcome in each intervention group; and the number of participants for whom the outcome was measured in each intervention group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting varies (medians, SEs, CIs, IQRs, ranges). Avoid misinterpreting SE as SD; where ambiguity exists seek clarification from study authors. There are algebraic relationships and methods to derive SDs from other reported statistics (see subsequent sections), but authors should be cautious and document transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining post-intervention values and change-from-baseline data
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies may report a mixture of post-intervention values and change-from-baseline measures; both can sometimes be combined in the same analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may extract both if available. Consider the potential for selective reporting (differences in choice of reported measure may associate with result direction/magnitude). Be cautious when baseline and post-intervention are reported for different numbers of participants (missing data/withdrawals), which complicates computing change scores. Seek evidence of selective reporting and document approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining SDs from SEs and confidence intervals for group means
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard deviation can be obtained from the SE of a mean by multiplying by the square root of the sample size. SDs can also be obtained from confidence intervals for group means using the appropriate divisor (e.g. 3.92 for large-sample 95% CIs) and adjusting for t-distribution for small samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the SE/CI relates to a within-group mean and not to a mean difference. For small samples (say <60 per group) use t-distribution critical values (lookup tables or software). Check that CIs are symmetrical around the mean—if not they may be on a transformed scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining SDs from statistics for differences in means (MD): P → t → SE → SD
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard deviations can be obtained when only statistics for the difference in means are reported, by converting P values to a t statistic (df = NE+NC–2), deriving SE of the MD as MD divided by t, and then deriving within-group SD from the SE (assuming equal SDs across groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exact P values are not available (only inequalities like P<0.05), use a conservative approach (take P at the reported upper bound). Exercise care in choosing which reported statistics refer to within-group versus between-group measures. Advice from a statistician is recommended when using these derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformations and skewed data
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies may present summary statistics after applying transformations (e.g. logarithms), such as geometric means and CIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect transformed results; meta-analysis may be performed on the transformed scale (e.g. log scale) and, if appropriate, back-transform for interpretation. SDs of transformed data can be derived from transformed CIs. Be mindful of skewness and choose methods appropriate to transformed distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interquartile ranges (IQR) to SD conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: IQRs describe the central 50% of observations. For large samples and approximately normal distributions, IQR width ≈ 1.35 SD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use the IQR→SD approximation when sample size is large and normality plausible. When distributions are skewed IQR cannot reliably estimate SD. Consider Wan et al (2014) sample-size-dependent extensions when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranges as measures of variability (not recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ranges are unstable and increase with sample size; they describe extremes rather than average variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on range→SD approximations (e.g. SD ≈ range/4) because the method is not robust. Walter & Yao and other methods exist but are limited; as a general rule, avoid using ranges to estimate SDs.

rubrics_metrics.name: No information on variability — imputing standard deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: When SDs cannot be derived and are not available from trialists, review authors may impute missing SDs (e.g. borrowing SDs from other studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imputation should be used sparingly. Borrowing SDs from other studies in the same review or other meta-analyses can be reasonable for a small proportion of studies, but avoid imputing when the majority of studies lack SDs. Consider using averages, highest, or 'reasonably high' candidate SDs; more complex methods (e.g. regression of log(SD) on log(mean)) exist. Perform sensitivity analyses to assess impact of assumptions; if many SDs are missing, consider narrative synthesis instead of imputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imputing SDs for change-from-baseline using correlation coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: When SDs for changes from baseline are missing, they can be imputed using a correlation coefficient (Corr) describing similarity between baseline and post-intervention measurements. Corr may be calculated from a detailed study or imputed from other studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate Corr from studies reporting baseline, final and change SDs; average group-specific correlations if appropriate. Use Corr to impute missing change SDs when baseline and post SDs are known. Use these methods sparingly because correlations vary with outcome, time interval and population; if Corr < 0.5, change-from-baseline analyses offer little benefit and post-intervention comparisons may be preferred. Document imputation choices and perform sensitivity analyses.
